Safe Work Australia, the national work health and safety policy agency, publishes two main
sources of national statistics:

- the **Traumatic Injury Fatalities (TIF)** database: every work-related death from a traumatic
  injury in Australia, compiled from coroners' records, regulator notifications, workers'
  compensation claims and media reports, and
- the **National Dataset for Compensation-based Statistics (NDS)**: accepted workers'
  compensation claims from every state, territory and Commonwealth scheme.

Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The three tables in `data/tidy/` hold every number in Safe Work Australia's published
detailed data files.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/intl-safework-australia/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), value = col_double(), level = col_integer(),
                            .default = col_character())) |>
    mutate(across(any_of("preliminary"), as.logical))
}

tif <- read_tidy("tif_fatalities.csv")         # worker deaths
nds <- read_tidy("nds_serious_claims.csv")     # serious workers' compensation claims
wcifr <- read_tidy("wcifr.csv")                # lost time claim frequency rates

# Most TIF tables come in calendar-year and financial-year versions; we use calendar years
tif_cal <- filter(tif, period_type == "calendar")
```

# Part 1. Work-related deaths over time

```{r tif-trend}
national_deaths <- tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "industry", level == 0) |>
  select(year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value)
national_deaths

ggplot(national_deaths, aes(year, rate_per_100000_workers)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2025) +
  labs(title = "Work-related traumatic injury deaths, Australia",
       x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000 workers")
```

**Questions**

# Part 2. Which industries are most dangerous?

```{r tif-industry}
industry_5yr <- tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "industry", level == 1, year >= max(year) - 4) |>
  select(category, year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(fatalities),
            # Rates are not published ("NP") for years with no deaths, so NA rates count as 0
            mean_rate = mean(replace_na(rate_per_100000_workers, 0))) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rate))
industry_5yr

industry_5yr |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_rate, fct_reorder(category, mean_rate))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths by industry, last 5 years",
       x = "Average deaths per 100,000 workers", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which three industries have the highest fatality rates? Which have the most deaths?
2. Health care and social assistance is Australia's largest employing industry, yet it has few
   deaths and one of the lowest rates. Agriculture has far fewer workers but many deaths. What
   does this tell you about using counts versus rates to set prevention priorities?
3. Agriculture, forestry and fishing has many self-employed workers. Why does that make the
   TIF a better source than workers' compensation claims for this industry?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. How do workers die?

```{r tif-mechanism}
tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "mechanism", level == 1, year >= max(year) - 4) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value)) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))

# Deaths in which a vehicle was involved
vehicles <- tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "vehicle type", level == 0) |>
  select(year, vehicle_deaths = value) |>
  left_join(select(national_deaths, year, all_deaths = fatalities), by = "year") |>
  mutate(share = vehicle_deaths / all_deaths)
vehicles

tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "vehicle type", level == 1, year >= max(year) - 4) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
```

**Questions**

1. What share of work-related deaths involve a vehicle? Which vehicle types are most common?
2. Many work-related vehicle deaths happen on public roads. Which agencies (besides work health
   and safety regulators) might be involved in preventing them?
3. Using the hierarchy of controls, propose one control for the most common type of vehicle death.

# Part 4. Serious workers' compensation claims

A **serious claim** is an accepted workers' compensation claim with **one working week or more**
of time lost from work. Claims are counted by the financial year they were lodged (July to June).
The most recent year is **preliminary**.

```{r nds-trend}
nds |>
  filter(breakdown == "industry", level == 0,
         measure %in% c("claims", "frequency_rate_per_million_hours")) |>
  select(period, preliminary, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value)

nds |>
  filter(breakdown == "nature", level == 2, measure == "claims") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  filter(max(value, na.rm = TRUE) > 6000) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = category)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Serious claims by nature of injury or disease (largest groups)",
       x = "Financial year ending", y = "Serious claims", colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. About how many serious claims are there each year? How does that compare with the number of
   deaths in Part 1?
2. Which type of injury or disease is most common? Which type has grown the fastest?
3. Most claims are injuries, not diseases. Why are occupational diseases under-represented in
   workers' compensation data?

# Part 5. Who is hurt and who dies?

```{r sex}
deaths_by_sex <- tif_cal |>
  filter(breakdown == "age and sex", measure == "fatalities", level == 2, year >= max(year) - 4) |>
  group_by(sex = category) |>
  summarise(n = sum(value)) |>
  mutate(outcome = "Deaths (last 5 years)")

claims_by_sex <- nds |>
  filter(breakdown == "age and sex", measure == "claims", level == 2, year >= max(year) - 4) |>
  group_by(sex = category) |>
  summarise(n = sum(value)) |>
  mutate(outcome = "Serious claims (last 5 years)")

bind_rows(deaths_by_sex, claims_by_sex) |>
  group_by(outcome) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

nds |>
  filter(breakdown == "age and sex", level == 1, measure == "incidence_rate_per_1000_employees") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = fct_inorder(group))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Serious claims per 1,000 employees, by age",
       x = "Financial year ending", y = "Claims per 1,000 employees", colour = "Age")
```

**Questions**

1. What share of work-related deaths are men? What share of serious claims are men? Why are
   these so different?
2. Which age groups have the highest serious claim rates? The README warns about the
   "65 and over" rate. Why?
